question_text: A company wants to add GenAI capabilities to an existing ERP system that uses SOAP/REST APIs and cannot be modified. Which integration pattern minimises coupling?

options.text: Directly couple the FM to the ERP database with read/write permissions
Build an event-driven integration layer: Lambda adapters translate between ERP SOAP calls and the Bedrock API, with EventBridge for loose coupling
Replace the ERP system with a modern platform before adding GenAI
Use Amazon Kendra to index ERP data and treat it as a search problem

explanation: Skill 2.3.1 describes API-based integrations with legacy systems and event-driven architectures for loose coupling. Lambda adapter functions translate between the ERP's protocol and Bedrock's API; EventBridge decouples producers from consumers so the ERP and GenAI layer evolve independently. Direct FM-to-DB coupling is a security and maintenance anti-pattern. Replacing the ERP is a multi-year project — not a GenAI integration approach. Kendra is being retired to new customers and is search-specific.

question_text: An enterprise wants employees to invoke Bedrock FMs using their existing corporate identity (Active Directory) without maintaining separate AWS IAM users. Which approach is correct?

options.text: Create individual IAM users for each employee and distribute long-term access keys
Configure AWS IAM Identity Center (SSO) to federate with the corporate IdP; employees assume an IAM role via SAML/OIDC to call Bedrock
Share a single IAM role credential across all employees
Embed AWS access keys in the application's front-end JavaScript code

explanation: Skill 2.3.3 describes identity federation between FM services and enterprise systems. IAM Identity Center (SSO) integrates with Active Directory via SAML or OIDC, allowing employees to assume time-limited IAM roles — no long-term keys needed. Individual IAM users with long-term keys are hard to manage at scale and violate least-privilege principles. Shared credentials eliminate per-user auditability. Embedding keys in front-end code is a critical security vulnerability.
source_topic: IAM Identity Center, identity federation, Bedrock access

question_text: A team wants a CI/CD pipeline for their GenAI application that automatically runs prompt regression tests, vulnerability scans, and supports rollback if quality checks fail. Which services should they use? (Choose TWO)

options.text: AWS CodePipeline for pipeline orchestration
AWS CodeBuild for build, test execution, and security scans
Amazon Kendra for indexing deployment artefacts
Amazon Polly for converting deployment logs to audio
Amazon QuickSight for pipeline dashboards

explanation: Skill 2.3.5 explicitly cites AWS CodePipeline and AWS CodeBuild for CI/CD pipelines with automated testing frameworks, security scans, and rollback support for GenAI components. CodePipeline orchestrates the stages (source → build → test → deploy); CodeBuild runs the actual build and test commands including prompt regression tests and security scans. Kendra indexes documents — not deployment artefacts. Polly is text-to-speech. QuickSight is BI visualisation, not CI/CD.
source_topic: AWS CodePipeline, CodeBuild, CI/CD for GenAI

question_text: A financial institution stores sensitive trading data on-premises due to regulatory requirements, but wants to augment GenAI responses with this data without ever sending it to the AWS cloud. Which approach satisfies both constraints?

options.text: Copy the data to Amazon S3 and use Bedrock Knowledge Bases normally
Use AWS Outposts to run Bedrock-compatible infrastructure on-premises, processing data locally
Anonymise all data before uploading to S3
Use a public third-party LLM API that supports on-premises data

explanation: Skill 2.3.4 cites AWS Outposts for on-premises data integration in cross-environment AI solutions. Outposts extends AWS infrastructure into the on-premises environment, allowing data to be processed locally without leaving the premises. Copying to S3 violates the 'no cloud transfer' constraint. Anonymisation may not satisfy strict regulatory requirements for certain data types. Third-party LLM APIs typically require cloud transfer.
source_topic: AWS Outposts, on-premises integration, data sovereignty

question_text: An organisation wants a centralised abstraction layer that provides observability, rate limiting, authentication, and model routing for all internal GenAI consumers. What pattern implements this?

options.text: Give every team direct Bedrock access with separate IAM policies
Deploy a GenAI gateway — API Gateway + Lambda — that centralises auth, rate limiting, logging, and model routing for all consumers
Use S3 presigned URLs to allow teams to call Bedrock
Publish a shared IAM role ARN for all teams to assume

explanation: Skill 2.3.5 describes centralised abstraction layers and observability/control mechanisms as part of secure GenAI gateway architectures. An API Gateway + Lambda gateway centralises: authentication (API keys/Cognito), usage plans and rate limiting, request/response logging, model routing, and cost attribution. Direct team access scatters governance. S3 presigned URLs are for object access — unrelated to Bedrock. A shared IAM role eliminates per-team auditability.
source_topic: GenAI gateway, API Gateway, centralised observability

question_text: An e-commerce platform wants to add a GenAI product recommendation feature to an existing microservices architecture without disrupting other services. Which integration pattern is most appropriate?

options.text: Embed the FM directly into the product catalogue microservice
Create a new GenAI recommendation microservice exposed via API Gateway; existing services call it over its REST API
Add the FM as a database trigger on the product catalogue table
Rewrite all microservices in a single monolith to include the FM

explanation: Skill 2.3.2 describes API Gateway microservice integrations for adding GenAI capabilities to existing applications. A new, isolated GenAI recommendation service with a well-defined API maintains separation of concerns, can be deployed and scaled independently, and minimises blast radius. Embedding the FM inside an existing microservice couples them together and complicates both services. Database triggers are not a GenAI integration mechanism. Monolith migration is counter to microservices principles.

topic: Lambda Durable Functions for long-running workflows
question_text: A company runs a multi-step AI document-review workflow: triage → wait for human expert input (up to 3 days) → generate final report. They want a fault-tolerant, serverless implementation that avoids managing state machines or containers. Which new AWS capability fits best?

options.text: Standard AWS Lambda (15-minute timeout) with DynamoDB polling for state
AWS Lambda Durable Functions — checkpoint-aware Lambda that can sleep for up to a year without incurring compute cost
AWS Step Functions Standard Workflow
Amazon ECS Fargate with a persistent container

explanation: AWS Lambda Durable Functions (launched re:Invent Dec 2025, Skill 2.3.1 — enterprise connectivity and Skill 2.5 — development tools) allows sequential, fault-tolerant workflows written as ordinary Lambda code that can suspend for up to ~366 days with no compute cost while waiting. It auto-checkpoints progress so failures replay from the last checkpoint — exactly right for a 3-day human-wait step. Standard Lambda has a 15-minute cap. Step Functions (C) also works for this pattern but requires writing ASL JSON state definitions — more operational complexity than Durable Functions. ECS Fargate incurs continuous cost even when waiting.
source_topic: AWS Lambda Durable Functions, long-running workflows

topic: AppSync GraphQL for multi-source AI queries
question_text: A GenAI dashboard needs to fetch FM-generated summaries, user chat history, and relevant document citations in a single API call to minimise round-trips. Which integration pattern is most appropriate?

options.text: Amazon API Gateway REST API with three separate endpoints, one per data source
AWS AppSync GraphQL API — resolves multiple data sources (Bedrock, DynamoDB, OpenSearch) in one query
An Amazon SQS queue that batches all three requests
AWS Step Functions calling each source sequentially

explanation: AWS AppSync is a managed GraphQL API that can resolve fields from multiple backends (Lambda calling Bedrock, DynamoDB for chat history, OpenSearch for citations) in a single client query, eliminating multi-round-trip overhead (Skill 2.3.2 — integrating AI capabilities into existing applications). REST APIs require separate requests per data source. SQS is asynchronous message queuing — not a synchronous multi-source query resolver. Step Functions calls services sequentially, not in a unified single response.
source_topic: AWS AppSync, GraphQL, multi-source FM integration

topic: AppConfig for dynamic FM selection without code changes
question_text: A team wants to swap the underlying foundation model powering their Bedrock application without redeploying code. New models are released frequently and the team needs to change the model ID in production within minutes of approval. Which AWS service enables this with no code deployment?

options.text: AWS AppConfig — store the model ID as a configuration value; the application reads it at runtime, so changing the config immediately takes effect without a code deployment
AWS CodePipeline — redeploy the Lambda on every model change
AWS CloudFormation — update the stack with the new model ARN each time
Hardcode the model ID in the Lambda environment variable and restart manually

explanation: AWS AppConfig allows configuration values (such as a Bedrock model ID) to be changed dynamically without any code deployment or Lambda restart. The application polls AppConfig at runtime and picks up the new value within seconds. CodePipeline and CloudFormation require deployment pipelines that take minutes and involve code/infra changes. Hardcoded environment variables require a manual redeploy.
source_topic: AppConfig, dynamic FM selection, feature flags

topic: SageMaker Custom Model Import to Bedrock
question_text: A data science team has fine-tuned a custom model in Amazon SageMaker and wants to serve it through the Amazon Bedrock API to benefit from managed serverless inference. What is the correct path?

options.text: Use Bedrock Custom Model Import to import the SageMaker-trained model into Bedrock, then invoke it via the standard Bedrock Converse or InvokeModel API
Directly call the SageMaker endpoint from the client using the Bedrock SDK
Export model weights to S3 and call them directly via a Lambda function
Re-train the model from scratch using Bedrock's fine-tuning job instead

explanation: Bedrock Custom Model Import lets teams bring custom models trained in SageMaker (or elsewhere) into Bedrock, unlocking serverless inference, IAM-based access, Guardrails, and the standard Bedrock APIs. Calling a SageMaker endpoint via the Bedrock SDK does not work — they are separate APIs. Calling raw weights via Lambda bypasses all Bedrock management features. Re-training from scratch discards the existing work.
source_topic: Bedrock Custom Model Import, SageMaker to Bedrock workflow
